idiom_name: impl std::ops::Add for Money { type Output = Money; }
implementation_notes: Rust expresses every overloadable operator as a trait, so closure is literally a trait implementation: impl std::ops::Add for Money with type Output = Money makes a + b yield Money, and the bound T: Add<Output = T> is the type-system statement of the pattern, which lets generic folds (Iterator::sum, reduce) work over your type. What replaces the classic structure is that trait implementation on an immutable struct whose operators take self by value - ownership makes the mutation-behind-a-closed-signature trap impossible - plus constructors that validate so each result satisfies the invariant. Prefer a named method (fn union(self, other: Self) -> Self) for combinations that are not additive; implement the reference variants as well when generic code must keep the operands alive.
pitfalls: i64 addition panics in debug builds but wraps in release, so a closed signature can hide an overflow; use checked_add and decide the failure policy explicitly.
Implementing Add only for owned values forces generic code to clone every operand; the standard library documents adding Add<&Money> implementations so that (a + b) style folds stay borrow-friendly.

Without a Sum/Default (or a zero constructor) implementation, iterator().sum() will not compile even though the operation is closed - supply the identity deliberately, not by defaulting money to 0 without a currency.
Deriving Copy on a value type is convenient but lets combinations be observed through stale copies; keep Copy only while the type is small and immutable.
